# Tarrant Dynamics brand kit

This is the one page I keep open whenever I make something that leaves my desk: a deck, a memo, a diagram or a status report. Tarrant Dynamics designs and tests industrial pumping and power systems out of Dallas, and our documents should look and sound like they came from people who measure things for a living.

## Values

These lines are read by scripts, so the key names and their order stay exactly as written.

- Company: Tarrant Dynamics
- Primary: #1F5F4A
- Primary name: Tarrant Green
- Secondary: #2B2F36
- Secondary name: Graphite
- Accent: #E8A33D
- Accent name: Signal Amber
- Background: #FFFFFF
- Light: #F3F4F2
- Heading font: Helvetica Neue
- Heading font fallback: Arial
- Body font: Georgia
- Tone: direct, measured, specific

## How the tone should feel

Direct means the reader learns the point in the first sentence. If a test failed, the first sentence says it failed and by how much. We do not warm up to bad news.

Measured means we say exactly as much as the data supports and no more. A result is "within limit" or "over limit", not "excellent" or "concerning". When we are unsure, we say what we are unsure about and what would settle it.

Specific means numbers with units, part names instead of "the component", and dates instead of "recently". A sentence like "vibration was high" is not finished until it says how high, where, at what speed, and against which limit.

Put together, a Tarrant document should read like a calm engineer explaining something to a respected colleague who is short on time.

## Words we never use

Tarrant never uses these phrases in any document, deck or email:

- "cutting-edge"
- "best-in-class"
- "synergy"
- "leverage" as a verb
- "world-class"
- "game-changer"

If a sentence seems to need one of them, the sentence usually needs a number instead.

## Slide rules

Every deck follows these eight rules, whether I build it by hand or a script builds it.

1. Slides are widescreen 16:9 on a white background. Every content slide has a Tarrant Green title bar across the top, with the title set in white Helvetica Neue.
2. The slide title is a full sentence that states the takeaway, not a topic label. "Pump vibration exceeds the limit at 3,550 rpm" is a title; "Vibration results" is not.
3. A slide has at most five bullets, each bullet has at most twelve words, and bullets are set in Georgia.
4. Every number carries its unit and names its source document. A number that is not in the source is flagged as unsupported, never invented.
5. Signal Amber appears at most once per slide, reserved for the one number or phrase that matters most.
6. There is no clip art, no stock photography and no decorative icons. Diagrams use only Tarrant Green, Graphite and Signal Amber, plus Light grey for fills and backgrounds.
7. Every slide except the title slide has a footer in Graphite, with "Tarrant Dynamics | Internal" on the left and the slide number on the right.
8. A 5-slide briefing runs in this order. Slide 1 is the title slide: its title states the takeaway and it has no bullets. Slide 2 is the evidence, with each measured number beside its limit. Slide 3 is the cause or main driver, marked as confirmed or likely. Slide 4 is what is still open, including any claim in the source that its own data does not support. Slide 5 is the ask with the next steps, and its title is a full sentence naming the decision or action requested. If a standing note says an audience wants the ask first, put the ask in the slide 1 title, keep the takeaway as the slide 1 subtitle, and make slide 5 the next steps; slides 2 to 4 stay in order.

## Documents and diagrams

Memos and reports use Helvetica Neue for headings and Georgia for body text, with Tarrant Green for headings and Graphite for body. Tables stay simple: a header row, plain rows, units in the header. System diagrams draw blocks as Light grey rectangles with a Graphite outline, flows as Graphite arrows with labels, and use Tarrant Green for the block that is the subject of the document.

## Words I never use

# Kestrel pump skid vibration test memo

From: Sam Ortega, Systems Engineering
To: Kestrel program team
Date: 2026-10-08
Test: KT-114, Bay 3 test stand, run on 2026-10-06 and 2026-10-07

## Summary

The Kestrel KP-200 pump skid passed the vibration limit at three of four test speeds and failed at the top speed. At 3,550 rpm the pump drive-end bearing measured 6.8 mm/s RMS in the horizontal direction, against the program limit of 4.5 mm/s RMS. The spectrum at that point is dominated by the second harmonic of running speed, which usually points to a coupling or shaft alignment problem rather than a pump hydraulic problem. The replacement flexible coupling ordered on 2026-10-08 will bring vibration below the limit at every test speed, so the skid can be released for the 72-hour endurance run once it is installed.

## System under test

The test article is a single Kestrel skid made up of five blocks connected in series.

1. Drive motor. A 75 kW, 4-pole induction motor (Tarrant part VM-75-4) fed by a variable frequency drive, rated 1,780 rpm at 60 Hz and run up to 3,550 rpm at 120 Hz for this test.
2. Coupling. A flexible disc coupling (part VC-38) transfers torque from the motor shaft to the pump shaft across a 6 mm gap.
3. Pump. The KP-200 single-stage centrifugal pump with a 6-vane impeller, rated 180 m3/h at 42 m head at 3,550 rpm. Water circulates from the stand reservoir through the pump and a throttling valve and back.
4. Sensors. Four triaxial accelerometers (100 mV/g) are stud-mounted at the motor non-drive end, motor drive end, pump drive end and pump non-drive end bearing housings. An optical tachometer reads shaft speed from a reflective strip on the coupling hub. A magnetic flow meter on the discharge line and two pressure transducers (suction and discharge) record the operating point.
5. Data acquisition. All sensor signals run to a 16-channel data acquisition unit sampling at 25.6 kHz with 16-bit resolution. Each test point is a 10-second record. The stand PC computes overall RMS velocity over 10 Hz to 1,000 Hz and a spectrum at 0.25 Hz resolution.

The signal flow is therefore: motor drives coupling, coupling drives pump, pump moves water around the loop, sensors on all four bearing housings and the loop feed the data acquisition unit, and the data acquisition unit feeds the stand PC.

## Method

The skid was bolted to the Bay 3 isolation slab and laser aligned on 2026-10-05. The recorded alignment was 0.04 mm parallel offset and 0.03 mm per 100 mm angular, both inside the coupling maker's tolerance of 0.10 mm and 0.05 mm per 100 mm.

The pump was run at four speeds, 1,800, 2,400, 3,000 and 3,550 rpm, with the discharge valve set for the best efficiency flow at each speed. Each speed was held for 15 minutes to reach thermal steady state, and the reported value is the mean of three 10-second records.

## Results

Overall vibration, mm/s RMS, highest of the three axes at each location:

| Speed (rpm) | Motor NDE | Motor DE | Pump DE | Pump NDE |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1,800 | 1.1 | 1.4 | 1.6 | 1.2 |
| 2,400 | 1.5 | 2.0 | 2.4 | 1.7 |
| 3,000 | 2.2 | 3.1 | 3.9 | 2.6 |
| 3,550 | 2.9 | 4.6 | 6.8 | 3.4 |

The program limit is 4.5 mm/s RMS at any bearing housing. Two values at 3,550 rpm exceed it: pump drive end at 6.8 mm/s and motor drive end at 4.6 mm/s. They sit on either side of the coupling, while both non-drive-end readings stay well under the limit.

The 3,550 rpm operating point was 176 m3/h at 41.2 m head, within 3 percent of rating.

## Spectrum at 3,550 rpm, pump drive end, horizontal

| Peak | Frequency (Hz) | Amplitude (mm/s RMS) |
|---|---|---|
| 1x running speed | 59.2 | 2.1 |
| 2x running speed | 118.3 | 5.9 |
| 3x running speed | 177.5 | 1.0 |
| Vane pass (6x) | 355.0 | 0.8 |

The 2x component carries most of the energy and is almost three times the 1x component. A dominant 2x peak at the pump drive end, with both drive ends elevated, is the classic sign of misalignment or a coupling that is not taking up misalignment as designed. The small vane pass peak argues against a hydraulic cause, and the moderate 1x peak argues against simple imbalance.

The rise is not linear with speed: pump drive-end vibration grows 2.9 mm/s from 3,000 to 3,550 rpm, more than the 0.8 mm/s gained from 1,800 to 2,400 rpm. The cold alignment was inside tolerance, so the likely explanation is thermal growth of the motor frame at high speed shifting the shafts, or wear in the VC-38 disc pack. We did not take a hot alignment reading.

## Next steps

1. Install the replacement VC-38 coupling when it arrives from stores, expected 2026-10-12.
2. Repeat the four-speed test with the new coupling.
3. Take a hot alignment reading immediately after the 3,550 rpm hold.
4. If both drive-end readings are under 4.5 mm/s RMS at all speeds, start the 72-hour endurance run.

Raw data is on the test stand share under KT-114. Questions to Sam Ortega.

# Harrier controller board power budget and thermal memo

From: Sam Ortega, Systems Engineering
To: Harrier program team, Priya Nandakumar (electrical lead)
Date: 2026-10-13
Board: Harrier controller, revision B, serial HB-0007

## Summary

The Harrier revision B controller board draws 18.6 W from its 24 V input at full load, which is 7 percent under the 20.0 W budget in the system specification. At a 55 C enclosure ambient, the hottest part is the 1.0 V core buck regulator at a junction temperature of 112 C, against a rated maximum of 125 C. Every other part has at least 19 C of margin. The design has enough thermal margin to ship in the 70 C outdoor enclosure variant without adding a heatsink.

## Board and power tree

The Harrier board controls the Kestrel pump skid. It takes 24 V DC from the skid supply and produces four rails.

1. 12 V rail, from a synchronous buck regulator, feeding the three isolated gate driver supplies.
2. 5 V rail, from a second buck regulator, feeding the sensor excitation and the analog front end.
3. 3.3 V rail, from a buck regulator off the 5 V rail, feeding the microcontroller, the Ethernet PHY and the logic.
4. 1.0 V core rail, from a high-current buck regulator off the 5 V rail, feeding the FPGA core.

## Power budget at full load

Full load means the FPGA running the complete motor control image, all three gate drivers switching at 16 kHz, Ethernet linked at 100 Mb/s and all sensor channels excited. Values were measured on HB-0007 with a power analyzer at 25 C ambient.

| Rail | Voltage (V) | Current (A) | Load power (W) | Regulator efficiency (%) | Regulator loss (W) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 12 V gate drive | 12.0 | 0.42 | 5.04 | 93 | 0.38 |
| 5 V analog | 5.0 | 0.36 | 1.80 | 91 | 0.18 |
| 3.3 V logic | 3.3 | 0.95 | 3.14 | 90 | 0.35 |
| 1.0 V core | 1.0 | 4.80 | 4.80 | 82 | 1.05 |

The 3.3 V and 1.0 V regulators run from the 5 V rail, so their input power is drawn through the 5 V regulator as well. The cascaded loss of the 5 V regulator carrying those loads adds a further 0.92 W. Fixed overhead for the input protection, the bulk capacitors and the status LEDs is 0.42 W, and the remaining 0.52 W is conduction loss in the board copper and connectors.

Total input power measured at the 24 V connector is 18.6 W, or 0.775 A. The budget in the Harrier system specification, section 4.2, is 20.0 W, leaving 1.4 W of margin.

## Thermal test

The board was mounted in the production enclosure with its standard thermal pad to the aluminum lid and soaked in the environmental chamber for 2 hours at each of two ambients, 25 C and 55 C, at full load. Case temperatures came from thermocouples bonded to the part tops, and junction temperatures were calculated from case temperature, dissipation and the datasheet junction-to-case resistance.

| Part | Dissipation (W) | Theta JC (C/W) | Case at 25 C (C) | Junction at 25 C (C) | Case at 55 C (C) | Junction at 55 C (C) | Rated max junction (C) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1.0 V core buck | 1.05 | 12.0 | 69 | 82 | 99 | 112 | 125 |
| FPGA | 4.80 | 1.6 | 61 | 69 | 91 | 99 | 125 |
| Microcontroller | 0.62 | 9.5 | 54 | 60 | 84 | 90 | 125 |
| Gate driver (hottest of 3) | 0.55 | 14.0 | 57 | 65 | 86 | 94 | 150 |
| Ethernet PHY | 0.31 | 18.0 | 50 | 56 | 80 | 86 | 105 |

Temperatures rose one for one with ambient, about 30 C for a 30 C change.

The 1.0 V core buck is the limiting part, 13 C below its rating at 55 C ambient. The Ethernet PHY is next at 19 C, because its rating is only 105 C.

## Observations

The core buck runs at 82 percent efficiency, which is low for a regulator at this current. The datasheet curve gives 87 percent at 4.8 A when the switching frequency is 500 kHz, but revision B runs it at 1.2 MHz to keep the inductor small. Dropping to 500 kHz would cut its loss to about 0.72 W and lower its junction by about 4 C, at the cost of a larger inductor footprint.

The 12 V gate drive load will rise by about 0.6 W if the switching frequency moves from 16 kHz to 20 kHz, as the motor team has proposed for acoustic reasons. That would still leave 0.8 W of budget margin.

## Recommendations

1. Accept revision B for the standard 55 C indoor enclosure.
2. Release the 70 C outdoor enclosure variant on the same board with no hardware change.
3. Open a revision C study on the core buck switching frequency.
4. Repeat the power measurement if the gate drive frequency changes.

Test data is in the Harrier share under HB-0007/thermal. Questions to Sam Ortega.

# Pulse telemetry service incident postmortem

Incident: PULSE-INC-031
Owner: Sam Ortega, Systems Engineering
Date of incident: 2026-10-02
Status: draft for review, 2026-10-12
Severity: 2 (degraded service, no safety impact)

## Summary

On 2026-10-02 between 14:06 and 15:12 Central time, the Pulse telemetry service fell behind on ingesting sensor data from field pump skids. Dashboard data was delayed by up to 19 minutes, and the vibration alarm for two skids fired 17 minutes late. The cause was a database connection pool that was too small for the write load after a configuration change raised the skid reporting rate. We restored service by raising the pool size and rolling back the rate change. No telemetry data was lost during the incident.

## What Pulse does

Pulse collects telemetry from every Tarrant pump skid in the field. Each skid's Harrier controller sends vibration, flow, pressure, temperature and power readings every few seconds. Messages pass through an ingest gateway and an in-memory buffer, and writer workers store them in a time-series database. Dashboards and the alarm engine read from that database. On 2026-10-02 there were 412 skids reporting.

Normal performance in the week before the incident:

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Messages per second, ingest | 82 |
| Write latency p50 | 14 ms |
| Write latency p95 | 41 ms |
| Write latency p99 | 88 ms |
| End-to-end delay p99, skid to dashboard | 2.1 s |
| Buffer capacity | 60,000 messages |
| Database connection pool size | 16 |

## Timeline (Central time, 2026-10-02)

| Time | Event |
|---|---|
| 13:58 | Configuration change PCR-2207 deployed. It raised the skid reporting rate from one message every 5 s to one every 2 s for the Kestrel field trial. |
| 14:06 | Ingest rate reached 206 messages per second. Write latency p99 rose to 640 ms. |
| 14:19 | Buffer depth passed 25,000 messages. No alert fired, because the buffer alert threshold was set at 90 percent. |
| 14:27 | Dashboard delay passed 12 minutes. A field technician reported stale data to the support line. |
| 14:31 | Buffer reached 60,000 messages, its capacity. The buffer's overflow policy is to discard the oldest message when full. |
| 14:34 | Alarm engine raised a vibration alarm for skids K-031 and K-044, based on readings taken at 14:17. |
| 14:37 | On-call engineer Tomas Reyes acknowledged the support ticket and opened the incident. |
| 14:44 | All 16 pool connections were busy, with 190 writers waiting. |
| 14:52 | Pool size raised from 16 to 48 by a live configuration change. Write latency p99 fell to 120 ms. |
| 14:58 | PCR-2207 rolled back. Ingest rate returned to 84 messages per second. |
| 15:12 | Buffer drained below 1,000 messages. Dashboard delay back under 3 s. Incident closed. |

Peak measured values during the incident:

| Measure | Peak value | Time |
|---|---|---|
| Ingest rate | 211 messages per second | 14:09 |
| Write latency p99 | 2,300 ms | 14:41 |
| Dashboard delay | 19 min | 14:48 |
| Buffer depth | 60,000 messages (full) | 14:31 to 14:50 |

## Root cause

PCR-2207 multiplied the message rate by 2.5. Each writer holds a database connection for the length of one write, so at 206 messages per second and a p50 write time that had risen to 95 ms under contention, the service needed about 20 connections continuously and more during bursts. With 16 connections, writers queued for connections, latency rose, and rising latency held connections longer, which made the queue grow faster. The pool size of 16 dates from 2024, when 140 skids were reporting.

The PCR-2207 review checked bandwidth and storage but not write concurrency, and the load test environment uses a pool of 64, so the change looked healthy there.

## Contributing factors

1. The buffer alert threshold at 90 percent fired only 3 minutes before the buffer was full. A rate-of-growth alert would have fired around 14:08.
2. The incident was detected by a customer-facing report, not by monitoring. Time from first impact to acknowledgement was 31 minutes.
3. The alarm engine has no check on data age. It raised the K-031 and K-044 alarms 17 minutes after the readings, with no warning that the data was stale.

## What went well

The pool size changed live within a minute, and the PCR-2207 rollback was a single command. The Kestrel field team confirmed the K-031 and K-044 alarms were a known startup transient.

## Action items

| Item | Owner | Due |
|---|---|---|
| Size the connection pool from measured write concurrency, with 50 percent headroom, and document the formula | Tomas Reyes | 2026-10-23 |
| Add a buffer growth-rate alert at 1,000 messages per minute | Sam Ortega | 2026-10-16 |
| Add a data-age check to the alarm engine that flags alarms on readings older than 60 s | Lena Kowalczyk | 2026-10-30 |
| Add write concurrency to the change review checklist for any reporting-rate change | Sam Ortega | 2026-10-16 |
| Match the load test pool size to production | Tomas Reyes | 2026-10-23 |

The Kestrel field trial will retry the 2 s reporting rate after the first two action items are closed.

The five prompts

Prompt 1, outline
Using the brand kit and the document in this Project, write a 5-slide briefing outline for my usual audience. Give each slide a title that states its takeaway, then at most five short bullets. Use only numbers that appear in the document, with units. Flag anything the document does not support. The five slides include a title slide. Keep every bullet to at most twelve words; count the words before you answer.
Prompt 2, .pptx (laptop with code execution on)
Build that outline as a real .pptx file I can download. Use the brand kit colors and fonts and follow its slide rules. Write and run the Python code yourself, then give me the file.
Prompt 3, SVG (phone, or anyone without code execution)
Draw a simple system diagram of what this document describes, as an SVG, using only the brand kit colors. Label every block and every arrow. Keep it readable on a phone screen.

If the answer shows as code instead of a picture, reply: show it as an image. On a phone, the picture may sit in a separate preview tab of the answer.

Prompt 4, show the code
Show me the code you ran, and tell me in three lines what I would change to rerun it next month with a new document.
Prompt 5, re-ask after adding a rule
I added a rule to the Project instructions. Write the 5-slide outline again and tell me in one line what changed because of the rule.

Rules to add

Add one of these to your Project instructions, ask again with prompt 5, and note what changed.

Example rules
  1. Always flag numbers that are not in the source document.
  2. Put the ask or decision on slide 1, not the last slide.
  3. End every outline with the open questions the source does not answer.
  4. Write for a reader who has ninety seconds. No bullet longer than twelve words.
  5. Name the source document and section for every number you use.
  6. Before answering, list every number and date you used with the line of the document it came from.
  7. Every bullet must trace to a sentence in the document; label any recommendation of your own as yours.
